title: Strings: the weakest cell sets the pace

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is one current draining all six tanks equally until the small tank empties first and turns red, driven backwards while the big tanks still hold charge, when you run the discharge on.
interactive.title: The string as tanks
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Six lead-acid cells sit side by side in series, each drawn as a tank. Five tanks hold 100 Ah. The sixth, a faded cell, holds an example 80 Ah. A small-cell stepper sets it to 60, 70, 80, 90 or 100 Ah. One current arrow runs through all six, because a series string gives the current one path. A mode switch sets Discharge, Charge or Float. On Discharge and Charge the current is an example 10 A, and an hours scrubber runs from 0 to 12 hours. Each hour every tank falls, or rises, by the same 10 Ah, whatever its size. A tank's level is the ampere-hours it holds, and the model fixes each tank's size at this current. On Discharge the small tank empties first. Past empty, the other five keep pushing the same current through it, the discharge way. It has nothing left to give, so the current drives it backwards. The model draws it red, holds it at empty and shows its voltage turned round. On Charge all six start flat. The small tank fills first. Past full it still passes the same current, which it turns into heat and gas, drawn as bubbles. On Float each tank shows its cell voltage instead. The charger holds the total at 2.23 V a cell, 13.38 V for six. A band from 2.18 to 2.33 V is drawn on each cell, 0.05 V below to 0.10 V above 2.23 V. An odd-cell slider sets the sixth cell's reading from 2.03 to 2.43 V. The other five share the rest of 13.38 V equally, so the total never moves. The second card shows two strings in parallel sharing a 100 A load. Each string is an example 10 mΩ. A cable slider for each sets its cable from 1 to 10 mΩ, starting at 2 and 6 mΩ. Both strings see the same volts, so the current splits inversely to each path's resistance. String A carries 100 × path B ÷ (path A + path B). The readouts are the ampere-hours through the string, what the small cell holds, and string A's current. On a phone the three readouts wrap onto a second line, and no word splits. Each show screen has under about 90 words. It ends on what its finished picture shows, so it reads well without the controls. Screen by screen. 0 shows the six tanks and the one current arrow. A 10 A load runs for 4 hours. Every tank falls by the same 40 Ah, whatever its size, because one current passes through each. It ends at 4 hours, the big tanks at 60 Ah and the small one at 40 Ah. 1 asks how many ampere-hours the small cell has given after those 4 hours. The choices are 40 Ah, 32 Ah, or less than 32 Ah because the big cells carry the load. The right pick says 'That's it: one current, so 10 A × 4 h = 40 Ah from every cell.' Hint for 32 Ah: that shares the load by size, but series gives one path, so every cell passes the same current. Hint for less: the big cells cannot pass current the small one does not, because it is the same current. 2 runs the load on to 8 hours. The small tank reaches empty, having given its 80 Ah. The big tanks still hold 20 Ah each, 100 Ah between them. The string cannot reach it, because every amp must pass the empty cell. So the string gives 80 Ah, not 100. It ends at 8 hours with the small tank empty. 3 says a string has five 100 Ah cells and one of 70 Ah, feeding 10 A. It asks how long it lasts. The choices are 7 hours, 9.5 hours or 10 hours. The right pick says 'That's it: the 70 Ah cell empties after 70 ÷ 10 = 7 hours.' Hint for 9.5: that averages the six cells, but the string stops when its smallest cell is empty. Hint for 10: that is the big cells' figure, and the small one runs out first. 4 keeps the load on past 8 hours. The five strong cells keep pushing 10 A through the empty one. It has nothing left to give, so the current drives it backwards and its voltage turns round. This is cell reversal, and it can leave the cell with a permanent short. In a long string one cell is a small part of the total, so the total can still look healthy. It ends at 10 hours, the small tank red. 5 asks what happens to the 80 Ah cell if the load stays on after it is empty. First choice: the others drive current backwards through it, and it can be damaged for good. Second: it rests at empty while the others carry on. Third: the others start to recharge it. Hint for rests: in series there is no way round it, so the current must pass through. Hint for recharge: the current still flows the discharge way, so it pushes the empty cell further, the wrong way round. 6 switches to Charge, with all six flat and 10 A flowing. Every tank rises by the same 10 Ah an hour. After 8 hours the small tank is full and starts to bubble. The big tanks need 20 Ah more each, so the current flows for 2 more hours. The full cell cannot store it, so it turns it into heat and gas. That is overcharge. It ends at 10 hours, all six full and the small one bubbling. 7 says the small cell is full after 8 hours of charging from flat. It asks what the current does in that cell for the next 2 hours. First choice: it turns into heat and gas, overcharging the cell. Second: it stops while the others catch up. Third: it flows round the small cell into the others. Hint for stops: one current flows through every cell, so if it stopped in one it would stop in all. Hint for round: series gives no way round, only through. 8 switches to Float. The charger holds 13.38 V, 2.23 V a cell. The odd cell sits in overcharge at an example 2.38 V, above the band. The other five share what is left, 2.20 V each, and are slightly starved. The total still reads 13.38 V, because the charger holds it there. It ends with the high cell in red and the total on target. 9 says six cells float at 13.38 V, right on target, and one cell reads 2.08 V. It asks whether the battery is healthy. First choice: no, that cell is 0.15 V below 2.23 V, outside the band. Second: yes, the total is right. Third: yes, 2.08 V is above the 2 V nominal. Hint for the total: the charger holds the total, so the other five rise to 2.26 V to make up the shortfall. Hint for nominal: on float each cell should sit near 2.23 V, and this one sits 0.15 V low. 10 shows the second card. Two strings of 10 mΩ share 100 A. String A's cable is 2 mΩ and string B's is 6 mΩ, so their paths are 12 and 16 mΩ. Both see the same volts, so the current splits inversely: 100 × 16 ÷ 28 = 57 A for A, and 43 A for B. String A works harder and empties first. Cable B then drops to 2 mΩ and the share evens to 50 A each. It ends with both cables at 2 mΩ. 11 says two 10 mΩ strings share 100 A, on cables of 2 and 8 mΩ. It asks what string A carries. The choices are 60 A, 50 A or 40 A. The right pick says 'That's it: paths of 12 and 18 mΩ, so A carries 100 × 18 ÷ 30 = 60 A.' Hint for 50: the load splits evenly only when the paths match. Hint for 40: that gives A the longer path's share, and more current takes the easier path. 12, 13 and 14 mix the ideas. 12 says two 12 V blocks in series each have an emf of 12.6 V behind 7 mΩ, and feed 100 A. It asks what the terminals read. The choices are 23.8 V, 24.5 V or 25.2 V. Hint for 24.5: that takes off only one block's 0.7 V, and in series the resistances add to 14 mΩ. Hint for 25.2: that is the emf, read with no current flowing. 13 asks whether two 12 V 100 Ah blocks store more energy in series or in parallel. First choice: the same, 2400 Wh either way. Second: series, because the volts double. Third: parallel, because the ampere-hours double. Hint for series: the ampere-hours stay at 100, so 24 × 100 = 2400 Wh. Hint for parallel: the volts stay at 12, so 12 × 200 = 2400 Wh. 14 says an equalise brings a low cell inside the band, but two days later it reads 0.15 V low again. It asks what that tells you. First choice: the cell itself is faulty, so trend it and test its capacity. Second: the equalise was too short, so repeat it until the cell holds. Third: the float is too low, so raise the charger's set point. Hint for repeat: every equalise overcharges the whole string, and long overcharge corrodes the good cells' grids. Hint for raising the float: that pushes every cell up, and the low cell would still lag.
interactive.ignores: Each tank's size is fixed. A real cell gives fewer ampere-hours at a higher current or in the cold, as lesson 3 showed. Charging is drawn ampere-hour for ampere-hour. A real recharge needs about a fifth more in than came out. The reversed cell is held at empty in red. A real reversed cell may partly charge the wrong way round, which a recharge must undo first. On Float the other five cells share the difference equally. Real cells each differ a little. The parallel card keeps both strings' voltages equal and fixed. Real strings drift as they discharge, which moves the share over time. Time is sped up.

explain.text:
Cells joined in series make a [[string]], and one current flows through every cell. So each cell gives the same ampere-hours, hour by hour. The cell that holds the fewest runs out first, and the string is finished when it is. Charged from flat, the same cell is full first. Either way, the weak cell is the one pushed too far.

Picture six cells as tanks. Five hold 100 Ah and one faded cell holds, say, 80 Ah. Draw 10 A. Every cell gives 10 Ah each hour, because the current has only one path. After 8 hours the small cell has given its 80 Ah and is empty.[^2] The big cells still hold 20 Ah each, but every amp must pass the empty cell to reach the load. So the string gives 80 Ah, not 100. Keep the load on and the five strong cells push the same current through the empty one. It has nothing left to give, so the current drives it backwards and its voltage turns round.[^3] This is [[cell reversal]]. It can leave the cell with a permanent short.[^7] In a long string one cell is a small part of the total. So the total can look healthy while one cell is being reversed.

A deep discharge can leave every cell flat. Charge the string from flat at 10 A and the story runs the other way. After 8 hours the small cell is full. The other five still need 20 Ah each, so the current keeps flowing. The full cell cannot store it, so it turns it into heat and gas.[^4] Kept up, that overcharge corrodes its positive grid, as lesson 4 showed. On float the charger holds the total, 2.23 V a cell, or 13.38 V for six. A weak cell can sit in overcharge. Its plates take no more charge, so its voltage climbs towards the gassing voltage of lesson 5. The total is fixed, so the strong cells share less and stay starved of charge.[^8] One maker allows each cell to sit 0.05 V below to 0.10 V above its float voltage, as long as the total is right.[^5] For 2.23 V that band runs from 2.18 to 2.33 V. Say the weak cell reads 2.38 V. The other five share what is left, 2.20 V each. The total still reads 13.38 V, because the charger holds it there. So the total cannot find a bad cell. Cell-by-cell readings can. That is how a battery can float at the right voltage and still fall short on a discharge test.

Strings can also sit side by side, in parallel. Their ampere-hours add and the voltage stays the same. Two blocks hold the same energy whichever way you join them. Parallel strings share the load like any parallel paths, inversely to resistance. Say two strings of 10 mΩ each share 100 A, one on 2 mΩ of cable and one on 6 mΩ. Their paths are 12 and 16 mΩ. So the first carries 100 × 16 ÷ 28 = 57 A and the second 43 A. The string on the short cable works harder and empties first. So makers ask for strings of the same capacity, design and age, with cables of equal resistance.[^6] The capacities and resistances here are examples, and the tanks treat each cell's ampere-hours as fixed. **Cells in series share one current, so the weakest cell empties first on discharge, fills first when charged from flat, and is overdriven either way.**

analogy.text: Think of a radial circuit run partly in a smaller cable. The same current flows through every length. So the smallest length sets what the whole circuit can carry, and it is the one that overheats if you push past that. A string works the same way. One current passes every cell, so the weakest cell sets what the string can give, and it is the one overdriven.
analogy.breaks: A cable stores nothing, so its limit is a current. A cell's limit is ampere-hours, so the weak cell limits how long the string runs, not how hard. And a cable never turns round, but an emptied cell can be driven backwards.

practice.text:
Use this when you read a string, test it, or join strings in parallel.

- On float, read every cell's voltage, not only the total. The charger holds the total, so the total hides a bad cell.
- Compare each cell with its maker's band. For one maker's vented cells that is 0.05 V below to 0.10 V above the float voltage.
- Note any cell outside the band, high or low, and read its specific gravity too.
- On a discharge test, watch the cell voltages as well as the total. A weak cell then shows before it is driven backwards.
- After an equalise or a boost, let the string stand for a few hours and read the odd cell again. A charge can cover a weak cell for a while, but the fault is likely to return within hours.[^9]
- Join strings in parallel only when they match in capacity, design and age. Run each on cable of the same size and length, so each path has the same resistance.

**Rule of thumb:** a series string gives the ampere-hours of its smallest cell. Parallel strings share the current inversely to their path resistance.

**Worked example:** A 12-cell string floats at 2.23 V a cell.[^43] So the charger holds 12 × 2.23 = 26.76 V. One cell reads 2.08 V. The other eleven share 26.76 − 2.08 = 24.68 V, about 2.24 V each. The total is right and eleven cells look normal. But 2.08 V is 0.15 V below 2.23 V, outside the band. That cell is the one to chase.

**Common mistakes**
- Judging a string by its total voltage.
- Expecting a string to give the average of its cells' ampere-hours.
- Taking a good reading straight after a charge as proof a cell is cured.
- Running parallel strings on cables of different lengths.
- Thinking series or parallel changes how much energy two blocks hold.

sources.title: Battery University | BU-803a: Cell Matching and Balancing
sources.quote: The weak cell holds less capacity and is discharged more quickly than their strong brothers.

sources.title: Battery University | BU-803a: Cell Matching and Balancing
sources.quote: Going empty first causes their strong brothers to overrun their feeble sibling to the point where a high load can push the weak cell into reverse polarity.

sources.title: Battery University | BU-803a: Cell Matching and Balancing
sources.quote: On charge, the weak cell reaches full charge first, and then goes into heat-generating overcharge, while the strong brothers still accept charge and stay cool.

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: Deviations of individual cell voltages of –0.05 to +0.10 V/c may be observed. However the total voltage of the battery shall be within the limits stated above.

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: In the case of parallel connected strings use batteries of the same capacity, design and age only with a maximum of 4 parallel strings. The resistance of the cables in each string must be the same, e.g. same cross-section, same length.

sources.title: Bu 502 Discharging At High And Low Temperatures — Battery University
sources.quote: Known as cell reversal, the weak cell gets stressed to the point of developing a permanent electrical short.

sources.title: Bu 403 Charging Lead Acid — Battery University
sources.quote: Weak cells may go into overcharge while strong cells remain in a starved state. A float current that is too high for the faded cell might sulfate the strong neighbor due to undercharge.

sources.title: Battery University | BU-803a: Cell Matching and Balancing
sources.quote: A charge may temporarily cover the deficiency, but the flaw will likely resurface again after a few hours due to the high self-discharge of the faulty cell.

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: The recommended float / charge voltage is 2.23 V/cell remove per cell at 20°C (68°F) depending on the specific type (see table 5). The charger voltage amounts to Uflo per cell x no. of cells (tolerance ± 1 %).
